item.title: Agentic AI Design Patterns and Visual Workflow Builders Gain Traction in 2026
item.description:
Agentic AI Design Patterns and Visual Workflow Builders Gain Traction in 2026

🔍 Overview

Agentic AI design patterns—reusable blueprints that tell an AI agent how to reason, act, and improve its own work—are becoming the core of production‑grade AI agents. 2026 sees these patterns packaged in frameworks like LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI, while visual workflow builders such as Workflow Builder, Dify, Langflow, n8n, and Sim make the engineering of complex agentic systems easier.

🧩 Core Agentic AI Design Patterns

  • Reflection – the agent drafts output, critiques it against clear criteria, then revises. It adds virtually no cost because it requires no new tools, only an extra pass. Research (Reflexion, Self‑Refine) shows that a weaker model wrapped in a reflection loop can beat a stronger model used zero‑shot.
  • Tool Use – the agent calls APIs, databases, or code to take action (e.g., running tests, reading failures, rewriting code).
  • Planning – the agent breaks a big goal into ordered steps and adapts when a step fails. Two common styles:
    • ReAct interleaves reasoning and action, choosing the next step after each result.
    • Plan‑and‑execute writes the full plan first, runs it, and replans only on failure.
  • Multi‑Agent Collaboration – specialised agents (researcher, coder, reviewer) split work and hand results to each other. Centralised coordination improved results by roughly 81 % on parallelisable tasks in Google Research tests, while poorly designed multi‑agent variants degraded performance by 39‑70 %.

⚙️ Implementations & Frameworks

  • LangGraph, Microsoft AutoGen, CrewAI – ship the four patterns as building blocks. Andrew Ng popularised the framing in 2024, and the same patterns appear in Anthropic’s guide to effective agents.
  • Production advice – combine two or three patterns: a core reasoning or planning loop, tools for action, and reflection for quality. Add multi‑agent setups only when sub‑tasks are genuinely independent. Cap retries at two or three and prefer external signals (unit tests, linters, schema validators) over self‑opinion.
  • Cost and risk – Gartner expects over 40 % of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027 due to rising costs, unclear value, and weak risk controls. The simplest pattern that solves the task is usually the right one.

📊 Choosing Visual Workflow Builders

Builder Primary Strength Ideal Use Case
Workflow Builder Embedded visual editor that lives inside a product Customer‑facing AI products needing an in‑app authoring layer
Dify All‑in‑one platform for building, testing, and deploying AI applications Internal AI products, prototyping, teams wanting a single system for the lifecycle
Langflow Rapid composition of agentic and RAG flows with strong Python ecosystem Python‑based agents and Retrieval‑Augmented Generation workflows
n8n Integration of AI agents with broader business automation Scenarios where agents sit inside existing automation environments
Sim Modern open‑source workspace with visual workflows, deployment, versioning Teams wanting open‑source flexibility and version control
Flowise (Archived) End of life announced August 2026; no longer a live option

Selection tips – Consider who will author the workflows, which system will handle execution, and how much control you need over the user experience and workflow data.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Gartner forecasts that 33 % of enterprise software applications will include agentic AI by 2028, up from under 1 % in 2024.
  • In production, a sound agent architecture (core reasoning/planning + tools + reflection) matters more than the underlying LLM model.
  • Visual workflow builders reduce the engineering burden by letting teams define, inspect, and change agent behavior without turning every adjustment into code.
  • Properly scoped patterns—using reflection for quality, planning for multi‑step tasks, and restrained multi‑agent collaboration—help keep token usage, latency, and cost under control while delivering reliable, testable AI agents.

#AIagents #AgenticAI #WorkflowBuilders #LLM

Source: Agentic AI Design Patterns | 4 Patterns to Know (2026) Source: Workflow Builder - Best visual workflow builders for AI agent applications in 2026 Source: Building Your Own AI Agent Server

item.title: Z.ai GLM 5.3 Model Now Available on Amazon Bedrock with Managed APIs
item.description:
Z.ai GLM 5.3 Model Now Available on Amazon Bedrock with Managed APIs

Z.ai’s GLM 5.3, a 753‑billion‑parameter mixture‑of‑experts model optimized for coding and long‑horizon agentic tasks, is now accessible through Amazon Bedrock’s fully managed inference service.

🔍 Overview

  • Modern coding and agentic workloads demand AI that can refactor repositories spanning hundreds of files, sustain multi‑hour agentic workflows without losing context, and reason through complex systems problems with tool use at every step.
  • Historically, meeting those demands with open‑weight models required provisioning and operating private inference infrastructure.
  • GLM 5.3 brings those capabilities to a managed environment, eliminating the need for customers to run their own hardware.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Model size: 753 B parameters, mixture‑of‑experts architecture.
  • Optimization target: Coding and long‑horizon agentic tasks such as multi‑step reasoning, tool‑augmented workflows, and sustained context across large code bases.
  • Coding performance: Reported competitive results on DeepSWE, Terminal Bench 3.0, and FrontierSWE benchmarks; 50 % improvement over GLM 5.2 on Z.ai’s internal coding benchmark.
  • Cyber‑security capability: Leading score of 84.5 on the CyberGym benchmark at release, positioning the model for defensive security workflows.
  • Agentic workflow demo: Used to run an authorized security test of a user’s application with Strix, an open‑source AI penetration‑testing agent.

🚀 Availability

  • GLM 5.3 is available to eligible enterprise customers on Amazon Bedrock.
  • Inference can be invoked via two cross‑Region profiles:
    • us.zai.glm-5.3 (US region)
    • global.zai.glm-5.3 (global region)
  • Service tiers:
    • Flex – cost‑optimized for less‑time‑sensitive workloads.
    • Standard – default balance of price and speed.
    • Priority – latency‑critical requests with higher price.
  • No infrastructure to manage; Bedrock securely routes requests to the chosen source region.

🛠️ How to Use

  • APIs: Accessible through OpenAI‑compatible Responses and Chat Completions APIs, as well as Bedrock Invoke and Converse APIs.
  • Prompt caching: Implicit (automatic) caching is enabled by default; explicit cache controls are recommended on the OpenAI‑compatible APIs. Caching reduces latency and input‑token cost for repeated calls that resend large system prompts or repository context.
  • IAM permissions required: bedrock:InvokeModel, bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream, and bedrock:CallWithBearerToken.
  • Console access: Prompts can be sent from the AWS Management Console without writing code or installing developer tools.
  • Programmatic access: Use the bedrock-runtime endpoint to call the model; OpenAI‑compatible APIs are recommended for new applications because they support a more complete feature set.
  • Credentials: Bedrock can generate API keys for OpenAI‑compatible integrations, but short‑lived credentials are preferred over long‑lived keys.

💡 Why it Matters

  • Reduced operational burden: Enterprises can leverage a 753 B model without provisioning their own GPU clusters.
  • Cost and latency improvements: Implicit prompt caching and selectable service tiers allow teams to balance expense against performance.
  • Enhanced security testing: The model’s strong benchmark performance on cyber‑security tasks enables realistic, AI‑driven penetration‑testing workflows like the Strix demo.
  • Scalable agentic applications: Designed for long‑horizon, tool‑augmented tasks, GLM 5.3 opens new possibilities for complex systems engineering and automated code‑base manipulation.

#AIModels #AmazonBedrock #CodingAI #CyberSecurity #AgenticAI

Source: Introducing GLM 5.3 on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Proposed Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy AI and Multimodal Systems
item.description:
Proposed Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy AI and Multimodal Systems

A new research paper proposes a unified evaluation framework designed to assess the trustworthiness of Large Language Models (LLMs), agentic systems, and multimodal models (MLLMs).

🔍 Overview

The framework was developed following a systematic mapping of 14,767 papers from arXiv submissions between January 2022 and August 2026. This analysis examined changes in:

  • Target systems and domains
  • Evaluation materials and conditions
  • Scoring mechanisms

Findings indicated a growing emphasis on professional applications, interaction, and action. While LLM-based scoring has increased for both agent and non-agent groups, model-generated materials have not shown a comparable sustained increase.

🧩 How it works

The framework connects cross-modal, trajectory-level, and output-level assessment through eight dimensions of trustworthiness:

Dimension Purpose
Capability Trustworthiness assessment
Robustness Trustworthiness assessment
Safety Trustworthiness assessment
Fairness Trustworthiness assessment
Transparency Trustworthiness assessment
Governance Trustworthiness assessment
Oversight Trustworthiness assessment
Efficiency Trustworthiness assessment

Additional technical features include:

  • Native Measurement Mapping: Preserves system-specific metrics while mapping them to common performance bands with traceable evidence and uncertainty estimates.
  • Meta-evaluation Layer: Examines the reproducibility, reliability, and validity of the evaluation.
  • Safety-critical Overrides: Prevents aggregate scores from masking critical failures.
  • Multidimensional Profiles: Used to expose specific strengths and weaknesses.

💡 Why it matters

The researchers state that benchmark scores alone are an incomplete basis for assessing the trustworthiness of modern AI systems. The proposed framework connects technical assessments with oversight needs by mapping to international standards, European Union regulatory requirements, and governance frameworks.

Empirical validation across deployment contexts is noted as an essential next step.

#LLM #AIEvaluation #AITrustworthiness #MultimodalAI #AgenticAI

Source: What Do We Expect from LLMs? Mapping the Design of LLM Benchmarks Source: A Unified Evaluation Framework for Trustworthy Large Language Models, Agentic AI, and Multimodal Systems

item.title: Understanding the Transition from Generative Chatbots to AI Agents
item.description:
Understanding the Transition from Generative Chatbots to AI Agents

AI agents represent a step forward from generative chatbots, marking a transition from reactive AI to AI that takes action by independently pursuing goals and developing solutions.

🔍 Overview

Chatbots and AI agents both serve meaningful use cases and can improve everyday work life, particularly in knowledge management for customer service and ITSM. While chatbots provide easy access to knowledge bases and answer user questions, AI agents are intended to simplify, accelerate, and make processes more consistent.

🧩 How it works

Chatbots

Chatbots are based on generative AI and rely on large language models (LLMs). They use machine learning (ML) and statistical patterns to generate natural language. They operate on a question-and-answer principle where the human user must provide precise, purposeful instructions—a practice known as prompt engineering—to obtain compelling results.

AI Agents

AI agents are specific applications of the overarching concept of agentic AI. An AI agent can be a piece of a larger agentic AI system that completes a sequence of tasks to pursue a goal. Unlike chatbots, agents:

  • Independently plan, reason, and complete multi-step tasks.
  • Act proactively rather than responding to questions.
  • Break tasks down into individual steps and make decisions on how to achieve a goal.
  • Adapt as needed and operate independently.

⚙️ Key details

Feature Generative Chatbots AI Agents
Core Function Describe possible paths to a solution Independently produce the solution
Approach Reactive (Question-and-Answer) Action-oriented (Autonomous goal pursuit)
Primary Focus Generating useful content Workflows and repetitive, routine processes

💡 Why it matters

AI agents can handle complex and dynamic processes. In ITSM, for example, they can independently analyze, prioritize, route, and resolve tickets. By focusing on routine processes, they prevent errors and free up human time for value-creating activities.

#AIAgents #GenerativeAI #ITSM #AgenticAI #MachineLearning

Source: AI Agents vs. Chatbots: Comparing Concepts

item.title: Campbell's Details New Agentic AI Engineer Role to Build Autonomous AI Systems
item.description:
Campbell’s Details New Agentic AI Engineer Role to Build Autonomous AI Systems

Campbell’s, the company behind brands such as the iconic Campbell’s, Pepperidge Farm, and Rao’s Homemade, has outlined the details and requirements for an Agentic AI Engineer position. The role is focused on designing, building, and deploying autonomous AI systems that can reason, plan, use tools, and execute multi-step workflows with minimal human intervention.

🔍 Overview

Unlike traditional AI/ML engineers who focus on model training and prediction, an Agentic AI Engineer orchestrates goal-driven workflows. These workflows integrate models, tools, memory, and business logic to dynamically achieve objectives.

⚙️ Key Responsibilities

The role involves designing, developing, and deploying generative AI and agentic systems. Below are the key responsibility areas for the position:

Responsibility Area Description
Design & Develop Agentic Systems Build intelligent agents capable of autonomous planning, reasoning, and task execution, often using LLMs (e.g., GPT-class, LLaMA), multi-modal models, and autonomous workflows.
Orchestration & Frameworks Implement agent orchestration using frameworks like LangChain, AutoGen, CrewAI, Semantic Kernel, or custom solutions.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Design and optimize RAG pipelines for enhanced reasoning with external knowledge, including document ingestion, chunking, embeddings, vector stores, and retrieval ranking.
Tool & Memory Integration Develop agents that call APIs, databases, and other tools, maintain memory, and adapt based on outcomes.
Evaluation & Monitoring Create evaluation frameworks for accuracy, grounding, latency, and cost; build observability for agent behavior and failure modes.
Model Adaptation Fine-tune or adapt foundation models (e.g., via LoRA, adapters) for domain-specific use cases.
Production Deployment Deploy GenAI/agentic systems in cloud-native environments with CI/CD, versioning, and runtime safeguards.
Cross-Functional Collaboration Work with data scientists, ML engineers, product teams, and governance/compliance stakeholders.

📋 Candidate Requirements

Candidates applying for the position must meet the following criteria:

  • 2+ years of experience in AI/ML system design, deployment, or autonomous agent development.
  • Proficiency in Python (and sometimes Java, C#) for AI/ML solution development.
  • Experience with agent orchestration frameworks and multi-agent communication protocols.
  • Hands-on experience with RAG architectures, evaluation methodologies, and LLM integration.
  • Experience with cloud platforms (e.g., Azure, AWS) and CI/CD pipelines.
  • Understanding of responsible AI, security, and compliance in regulated domains such as retail.

💼 Company Benefits

Campbell’s offers a comprehensive support package for employees starting on day one:

  • Medical, dental, short and long-term disability, AD&D, and life insurance for individuals, families, and domestic partners beginning on day one.
  • Immediate vesting and eligibility to enroll in a matching 401(k) plan on the first day of employment.
  • Unlimited sick time alongside paid time off and holiday pay.
  • Free access to the fitness center for employees located at World Headquarters (WHQ).
  • On-site day care operated by Bright Horizons and access to a company store.
  • Donation and volunteer matching up to $1,500 annually through the “Campbell’s Cares” program.
  • Support from a variety of Employee Resource Groups (ERGs).

#Campbells #AgenticAI #AIJobs #MachineLearning

item.title: CHIME Improves Long-Horizon Agent Planning Using Credit-Aware Memory Evolution
item.description:
CHIME Improves Long-Horizon Agent Planning Using Credit-Aware Memory Evolution

Researchers have introduced Credit-Aware Hierarchical Memory Evolution (CHIME), a framework designed to enhance agentic planning capabilities without requiring parameter updates.

🔍 Overview

Planning allows agents to decompose complex tasks into manageable steps, but existing methods often face high inference costs or the credit assignment problem, where noisy outcomes conflate plan quality with environmental factors.

🧩 How it works

CHIME utilizes an attribute-before-memorize principle to ensure that only relevant experience is stored in its external memory bank. The system operates as follows:

  • Maintains separate banks: A dedicated planning bank and an execution bank.
  • Attribution process: Each task outcome is attributed to the plan, the execution, both, or neither.
  • Selective updating: Only the specific bank corresponding to the identified source of success or failure is updated.

⚙️ Key details

Experimental results on four long-horizon agent benchmarks demonstrate that CHIME outperforms existing state-of-the-art training-based and self-evolving memory baselines.

Capability Feature Outcome
Memory efficiency Accumulates effective memory with far fewer items
Performance Learned memory values faithfully reflect downstream utility
Memory priority High-quality planning memories are more valuable than execution memories
Transferability Memory effectively transfers across backbone models

🚀 Availability

Code for CHIME will be released via a future link.

#AI #MachineLearning #LLM #AgenticAI

Source: CHIME: Credit-Aware Hierarchical Memory Evolution for Long-Horizon Agentic Planning Source: MASkills: Continual Skills Optimization for Multi-Agent LLM Systems Source: WMLLM: Self-Evolving Optimization Agents via Predict-Then-Act World Modeling

item.title: Cost‑saving techniques cut LLM spend for agentic AI workflows
item.description:
Cost‑saving techniques cut LLM spend for agentic AI workflows

ProjectDiscovery applied this to their security testing agent Neo in April 2026. The result was a 59 percent reduction in LLM costs within the first few days, reaching 70 percent by day ten.

🔍 Overview

  • “An agent runs a loop: it reasons, calls a tool, reads the result, updates its plan, and repeats.”
  • “Every iteration carries the full conversation history forward.”
  • “By step five of a ten-step task, the model is reading everything that came before it on every single call.”
  • “Context length grows with each step, and cost scales with context length.”

📊 Cost Challenge

  • “According to research from Antino and Zylos, LLM API calls account for 70 to 85 percent of total agentic AI cost, and agents make three to ten times more LLM calls than simple chatbots.”
  • “Unoptimized production agents regularly reach $10 to $100 per session in API spend.”
  • “That ceiling matters because 88 percent of organisations are experimenting with agents, but only 23 percent are actively scaling, and Gartner projects 40 percent of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027.”

📏 Measuring First

  • “You cannot optimise what you have not measured.”
  • “Instrument every LLM call before you write a single optimisation.”
  • “Record input tokens, output tokens, model name, task type, and step number.”
  • “Aggregate by task run, not by request, so you can see the full cost of one unit of work.”
  • “If your cost‑per‑task spikes after step three, that tells you the context is accumulating faster than the task is progressing, which points directly at context compaction as the right fix.”
  • “Store these records somewhere you can query them by task type.”
  • “After one week of load testing, you will have a cost distribution per task type that you can use to set per‑task budgets and to forecast monthly spend at your target volume.”

💾 Prompt Caching

  • “If your system prompt is long, your agent pays full price for it on every call.”
  • “Prompt caching lets the model provider store the computed representation of a static prefix and charge a fraction of the normal input rate for subsequent calls that reuse it.”
  • “The technique requires that the cacheable content sits at the start of the prompt and stays stable across calls, so structure your prompts with the static system instructions first and the variable task context after.”
  • “One developer account dropped from $720 per month to $72.”

🧩 Model Routing

  • “Not every step in an agentic workflow needs a frontier model.”
  • “Planning and synthesis benefit from the best reasoning available.”
  • “Classification, intent detection, filtering, and repeated sub‑tasks often produce equally reliable results from a model that costs a tenth as much.”
  • “Build a routing layer that maps task types to model tiers.”
  • “The decision criterion is whether the step requires open‑ended reasoning or whether it fits inside a well‑defined scope where a smaller model can be reliable.”
  • “Test each route with representative inputs before you trust it in production.”

🛠️ Context Summarisation

  • “The most direct attack on the quadratic growth problem is to stop the context from growing unchecked.”
  • “At each step, summarise completed sub‑tasks into a compact record and drop the raw turn history.”
  • “This requires a small summarisation call, which adds a modest cost at each checkpoint, but that cost is fixed per step rather than proportional to total history length.”
  • “For tasks beyond five or six steps, compaction almost always pays for itself.”

#LLM #AgenticAI #PromptCaching #CostOptimization

Source: Agent Token Economics: Engineering Cost Efficiency Before Your First Production Deployment — Agentic Ready

item.title: Atos and AWS partner to upskill 400 engineers in agentic AI development
item.description:
Atos and AWS partner to upskill 400 engineers in agentic AI development

Atos recently completed an intensive upskilling initiative for 400 engineers focused on practical agentic AI development through a partnership with AWS.

🔍 Overview

Atos addressed the challenge of building real-world agentic AI capability beyond theoretical knowledge by partnering with AWS in 2026. They ran a three-day competitive event using AWS AI League and Workshop Studio, enabling engineers to progress from foundational skills to deploying multi-agent systems with pathfinding, guardrails, memory, and fine-tuned models.

🧩 How it worked

Engineers participated in a gamified challenge where they built autonomous AI agents to navigate a dungeon maze. Agents had to:

  • Find paths through maps
  • Solve tile challenges
  • Avoid traps
  • Reach treasure within time/life limits

Scoring combined performance (correct answers, coin collection, map completion) and efficiency (concise responses, life retention). Teams competed on a live leaderboard.

⚙️ Key details

  • Participant experience levels: 5% no prior knowledge, 25% basic awareness, 50% theoretical understanding (no hands-on), 20% practical experience.
  • Event structure:
    • 2-hour kick-off workshop
    • Daily 1-hour office hours
    • 1-hour finale for top 3 teams

🧱 Core components

item.title: Harness engineering emerges as key to AI agent performance
item.description:
Harness engineering emerges as key to AI agent performance

A new discipline called harness engineering is shaping how language models are turned into functional agents. Early 2026 leaderboards show that the harness—software scaffolding around a model—can influence performance as much as the model itself.

🔍 Overview

Harness engineering is the discipline of designing the software that surrounds a language model and turns it into a working agent. It covers context delivery, tool interfaces, memory, and sandboxes. The model supplies the reasoning, while the harness decides what the model sees, what it can do, what it remembers, and where it runs.

⚙️ Key details

  • An agent harness is the software scaffolding around a model.
  • Anthropic describes it as ’the loop, tools, context management, and guardrails that turn raw intelligence into a working agent'.
  • METR called it scaffolding back in 2023: scaffolding plus a model equals an agent.

Performance impact

  • On early 2026 leaderboards, the harness moved the score at least as much as the model did.
  • On the Terminal-Bench 2.0 leaderboard, Claude Opus 4.6 scored between 58.0% and 74.7% across seven harnesses, all submitted between 5 and 23 February 2026.
    • The highest of the seven was Terminus-KIRA from KRAFTON AI at 74.7%.
    • Confidence intervals sit near plus or minus 2.5 to 2.9 points, so a 16.7 point spread is not noise.
  • On SWE-bench Verified’s bash-only board, nine frontier models ran the identical mini-swe-agent scaffold at matched reasoning effort, all submitted on 17 February 2026. Their scores spanned just 66.6% to 76.8%, a 10.2 point gap.
  • On the newer Terminal-Bench 2.1 board, harness spreads collapse to between 0.2 and 8.1 points once reasoning effort and submission dates are matched, so the gap appears to be narrowing.

Components

  • Tool interfaces: Tool dispatch turns a model’s request into a real action. The model returns a tool-use block, the harness runs it and returns the result, and the loop repeats until the model stops asking.

    • The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how an agent reaches those tools, and calls itself ‘an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems’.
    • Anthropic created MCP and donated it to the Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025.
    • The MCP specification warns that tools ‘represent arbitrary code execution’.

  • Memory: State persistence is how an agent survives its own context window.

    • Context compaction is the usual answer, and the Claude Agent SDK summarizes earlier messages as the limit approaches.
    • Compaction is lossy, and Anthropic says so: ‘While compaction preserves continuity, it doesn’t give the agent a clean slate.’
    • Durable state therefore belongs outside the transcript: Claude Code re-injects project memory files after compaction, and LangGraph gives agents short-term memory through checkpointers and long-term memory through stores.

  • Sandboxes: A sandbox is the boundary between a mistake and an incident.

    • Claude Code’s built-in sandbox uses Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap plus socat on Linux and WSL2, and by default a command writes only to the working directory and the session temp directory.
    • OpenAI Codex offers read-only, workspace-write and danger-full-access modes, runs with network off by default, and applies one rule: ‘deny always wins over allow.’
    • Heavier isolation goes as far as microVMs such as Firecracker, and E2B says its same-region sandboxes ‘start in less than 200 ms’.

  • Guardrails: Guardrails decide what an agent may attempt, and isolation decides what the attempt can reach.

    • Anthropic draws the line cleanly: ‘Permission modes decide whether a tool call runs and whether you are prompted first. Isolation restricts what a command can access once it runs.’
    • Claude Code ranks its permission modes from Manual up to bypassPermissions, with acceptEdits, plan, auto and dontAsk in between, and deny rules block in every one of them.
    • The OpenAI Agents SDK adds input, output and tool guardrails, any of which can raise a tripwire and halt the run.

💡 Why it matters

  • The core difference is scope: prompt engineering shapes one exchange with a model, while harness engineering shapes the system around the model for the length of a task.
  • Neither replaces the other: a harness contains prompts, and a bad system prompt sinks a good agent.
  • Coding agents are where harness engineering stopped being optional.
  • OpenAI’s account of adopting Codex is blunt about why: ‘Early progress was slower than we expected, not because Codex was incapable, but because the environment was underspecified.’

🧩 How it works

  • Anthropic defines context engineering as ’the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens (information) during LLM inference'.

#AIagents #harnessengineering #LLMs #agenticAI #MCP #sandboxing

Source: What is Harness Engineering? The AI Agent Scaffolding Guide

item.title: 🔍 Bot Scanner: Building the 'Skyscanner' for LLM Answers in the Agentic AI Era
item.description:
🔍 Bot Scanner: Building the “Skyscanner” for LLM Answers in the Agentic AI Era

📊 Summary

Bot Scanner emerges as a revolutionary platform that queries multiple LLMs simultaneously and uses AI judges to rank their responses—effectively creating a “Skyscanner for AI answers” that saves time and improves decision-making in our increasingly complex AI ecosystem. This 5-minute read explores how this tool transforms LLM response evaluation and why it matters for the emerging agentic AI landscape.

🚀 The Paradox of AI Choice Paralysis

In today’s rapidly evolving AI landscape, we face a peculiar dilemma: more choice, more confusion. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek—the list grows daily. Each model excels at different tasks, leaving us with the nagging question: “𝘐𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘰𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘣𝘭𝘦 𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘸𝘦𝘳 𝘧𝘰𝘳 𝘮𝘺 𝘴𝘱𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘧𝘪𝘤 𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘤𝘢𝘴𝘦?”

Many applications now offer side-by-side LLM comparisons, but they still require 𝙮𝙤𝙪 to manually evaluate each response—a tedious process reminiscent of booking flights by visiting individual airline websites. 🛫

Enter Bot Scanner: a platform that not only queries multiple language models with a single prompt but crucially employs other AI models to evaluate and rank those responses. It’s the meta-AI solution we’ve been waiting for, offering a simple chatbot-like interface that hides sophisticated evaluation machinery.

🧠 How Bot Scanner Works: AI Evaluating AI

Bot Scanner operates through an elegant two-step process:

  1. Broadcast Phase 📢 — Your prompt is sent to multiple “responder” LLMs that you select
  2. Evaluation Phase ⚖️ — Responses are passed to your chosen “ranker” LLMs that judge quality and produce a ranked list

This architecture provides unprecedented control over the evaluation chain—from selecting the contestants to appointing the jury. Think of it as creating a custom AI talent show where you choose both the performers and the judges! 🏆

1

User Prompt → [Responder LLMs] → Multiple Answers → [Ranker LLMs] → Ranked Results

The 𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗳𝗶𝘁𝘀 are immediately apparent:

  • ⏱️ Time Efficiency: No more manual sifting through multiple outputs
  • 🎯 Better Decisions: Quickly identify high-quality responses based on criteria evaluated by trusted AI judges
  • 🛠️ Agent Optimization: For developers building AI agents, Bot Scanner helps select the optimal “expert” LLMs for each component task

🔄 The Evolution: From AutoBench to Bot Scanner

Bot Scanner didn’t emerge from a vacuum. Its genesis lies in AutoBench, an advanced benchmarking framework developed by eZecute that pioneered the “Collective-LLM-as-a-Judge” paradigm.

🧩 The traditional benchmarking approach has significant limitations:

  • Static datasets quickly become outdated
  • Models can be fine-tuned to game specific benchmarks
  • Human evaluation doesn’t scale efficiently

AutoBench addressed these issues by using a collective of AI models to evaluate other AIs—a method specifically designed to be “ASI-ready” (Artificial Superintelligence ready), capable of assessing LLMs even when they surpass human evaluation capabilities.

The team behind AutoBench, including collaboration with AI researchers like Marco Trombetti and support from companies like Transalted, realized that this sophisticated evaluation system could be packaged into an accessible tool for everyday use.

𝙏𝙝𝙚 𝙧𝙚𝙨𝙪𝙡𝙩? Bot Scanner. 🎉

🤖 The Agentic Era: Why Evaluation Matters More Than Ever

We’re rapidly approaching what experts call the “agentic era” of AI—where systems autonomously execute complex, multi-step tasks with minimal human guidance. This evolution brings a unique challenge: how do we ensure these agents consistently deliver effective results aligned with our intentions?

This shift requires us to rethink the traditional “Mixture of Experts” (MoE) paradigm. Rather than internal neural sub-networks, we’re seeing systems where distinct, specialized LLMs collaborate like a team of experts. Imagine a market research agent where:

  • One LLM excels at data retrieval 📊
  • Another specializes in sentiment analysis 🧐
  • A third focuses on creative brainstorming 💡

While powerful, this “multi-LLM agent” approach makes evaluation exponentially more complex. How do you select the right AI “expert” for each sub-task?

Bot Scanner offers a solution by providing real-time, task-specific evaluation that can guide these choices. It’s not just about comparing models—it’s about building better AI systems through informed selection.

💎 Bot Scanner: A Specialized Tool for Critical Decisions

It’s important to understand what Bot Scanner is—and isn’t.

Bot Scanner isn’t a replacement for everyday chatbots like ChatGPT or Gemini. Instead, it’s a specialized tool for situations where accuracy and quality across multiple models are paramount. This depth comes at a computational cost; a single query might involve hundreds of LLM calls, making it up to 100 times more expensive than standard LLM queries.

Similarly, Bot Scanner isn’t a general benchmarking system. Rather than providing broad performance metrics across thousands of interactions, it delivers immediate, question-specific rankings focused on your exact use case.

🔮 The Future is Continuously Evaluated

As AI systems become more powerful and autonomous, the need for robust, dynamic evaluation will only grow. Static benchmarks will continue to serve their purpose, but tools like Bot Scanner represent the necessary evolution toward context-aware, user-driven evaluation.

The ultimate goal? To give everyone—from individual researchers to large teams—accessible means to navigate the increasingly complex AI landscape and make better-informed decisions about the AI they deploy.

The question isn’t whether we’ll need tools like Bot Scanner—it’s how quickly we can integrate this meta-evaluative approach into our AI development and usage workflows. As models continue multiplying and specializing, will you still manually compare outputs, or leverage AI itself to identify the best responses for your specific needs? 🤔

item.title: 🧬 AI Agents Transforming Life Sciences: How Data is Powering the Next Healthcare Revolution
item.description:
🧬 AI Agents Transforming Life Sciences: How Data is Powering the Next Healthcare Revolution

𝗦𝘂𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆: At the 7th Annual AWS Life Sciences Symposium, industry leaders revealed how generative and agentic AI are revolutionizing healthcare innovation. This article explores how leading companies are unifying data silos, deploying real-world evidence, and implementing AI agents that accomplish in minutes what previously took days—while highlighting practical tools any organization can leverage today.

🔬 The AI Revolution in Life Sciences Has Arrived

When over 1,000 life sciences industry leaders converge to discuss technology’s future, patterns emerge. At the recent AWS Life Sciences Symposium in New York City, one message resonated across all 26 sessions: generative AI has moved beyond experimentation into delivering tangible results, with the life sciences sector leading this transformation.

The symposium revealed a pivotal shift—organizations are no longer pursuing AI initiatives for innovation’s sake. Instead, they’re strategically scaling proven solutions that deliver measurable outcomes in research, clinical trials, manufacturing, and commercial operations.

But what’s the secret ingredient behind successful AI implementation? The answer was unanimous: 𝙙𝙖𝙩𝙖.

📊 Data as the Ultimate Differentiator

“Your AI is only as smart—and as strategic—as the data behind it.”

This statement encapsulates perhaps the most critical insight from the symposium. Companies achieving breakthroughs aren’t necessarily those with the most sophisticated AI algorithms, but rather those who’ve successfully transformed fragmented data into unified strategic assets.

AWS categorizes this data into three critical buckets:

  • Your existing data
  • New data you create
  • Third-party data

The symposium showcased how Merck Research Labs exemplifies this approach. Their team created a clinical data layer on AWS that consolidates clinical and operational information across studies onto a single platform, enabling automation that dramatically accelerates processes.

Another game-changing element is real-world data (RWD). Consider this striking statistic: 85% of FDA drug approvals between 2019-2021 leveraged real-world evidence. Despite its proven value, working with RWD has historically been slow and frustrating—taking up to four months to process. AWS partnerships have reduced this timeline to as little as two weeks.

📸 Imagine a data pipeline visualization showing the transformation from months-long processes to weeks

The collaboration between AWS, the Broad Institute, and Manifold AI further illustrates this data revolution. This partnership combines seamless data access with advanced analysis capabilities using AWS HealthOmics, Amazon Bedrock, and Anthropic’s Claude to power AI-driven research at unprecedented scales.

🤖 From Experiments to Excellence: Scaling What Works

A clear trend emerged from the symposium: forward-thinking organizations have moved beyond random AI experiments to strategically scaling successful use cases.

Johnson & Johnson’s approach exemplifies this shift. The company has pivoted to focus exclusively on their highest-value AI applications—a strategy that enables faster ROI, better resource allocation, and sustainable innovation.

Sanofi provided another compelling case study. Their AI-powered assistant “Concierge” delivers contextual answers about company policies and procedures. The impressive adoption rate—over 80% of Sanofi employees—demonstrates how deeply AI can integrate when it solves genuine daily challenges.

The most successful implementations target specific high-impact challenges. Working with PwC, AWS identified several use cases delivering significant value:

  • 🔍 Biomarker Discovery: AI agents mining literature and first-party data
  • 📋 Regulatory Amendment Analysis: Reducing costly protocol amendments through AI-powered feedback analysis
  • 🧪 Clinical Trial Analysis: AI-guided exploration accelerating insights
  • 🏭 Manufacturing Execution System Chat: Natural language interfaces extracting actionable intelligence
  • 💼 Sales Concierge: Supporting commercial teams with timely, relevant data
  • 🔐 Fraud Detection: AI-driven anomaly detection in drug pricing programs
  • 📈 Protocol Generation: Accelerating clinical trial design through AI-assisted drafting

To facilitate adoption, AWS has created the Life Sciences Generative AI Portal—a curated collection of over 40 generative AI demos and customizable prototypes already delivering value across R&D, clinical development, manufacturing, and commercial operations.

🧠 The Next Frontier: Agentic AI in Action

Perhaps the most exciting developments centered around 𝙖𝙜𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙞𝙘 𝘼𝙄—AI systems that can independently perform complex sequences of tasks to achieve specific goals.

Genentech showcased this potential with a striking example: A distinguished scientist completed a complex analysis of cell surface receptors in just 10 minutes using agentic AI—a task that previously required two full days of work.

To accelerate adoption across the industry, AWS recently introduced an open-source agentic AI toolkit built on Amazon Bedrock. This toolkit includes:

  • Research Agents: For target identification, biomarker discovery, and experimental design
  • Clinical Agents: Supporting trial analysis, protocol optimization, and patient stratification
  • Commercial Agents: Generating competitive intelligence and market insights

📸 Conceptual illustration of multiple AI agents working together to solve complex research problems

Publisher Wiley collaborated on an agent capable of searching full-text articles published under creative commons licenses. This agent delivers reliable, cited insights in minutes rather than the hours or days typically required for literature review—a transformational time-saving tool for researchers.

The toolkit’s architecture allows individual agents to connect with multi-agent supervisors using Amazon Bedrock’s collaboration capabilities, enabling developers to orchestrate across agents and build sophisticated workflows.

🚀 Building on a Foundation for Future Innovation

The symposium made clear that while technology continues advancing at breakneck speed, success depends on establishing a scalable, secure data foundation. This foundation enables organizations to adapt and evolve regardless of what innovations emerge next.

The life sciences industry stands at an inflection point where AI is transitioning from experimental to essential. Organizations that unify their data, implement strategic AI use cases, and embrace agentic capabilities are positioned to lead the next wave of healthcare breakthroughs.

What will your organization’s AI strategy prioritize in this rapidly evolving landscape? Will you focus on data integration, specific use case implementation, or exploring agentic capabilities?
